name: Rogalin Palace
region: Greater Poland Voivodeship (Wielkopolska) — Rogalin village, near Mosina, Poznań County
address: Pałac w Rogalinie, Rogalin 4, 62-022 Rogalin, Poland
architectural_style: Baroque palace with neoclassical elements, late 18th century, with English landscape park — built for Kazimierz Raczyński, Voivode of Greater Poland, in the late 18th century; the main palace building is a Baroque composition in the tradition of Central European aristocratic residences; the flanking wings and service buildings were added in the early 19th century; the palace grounds include a formal French garden adjacent to the building and an extensive English landscape park with the famous ancient oak grove; the coach house adjacent to the palace was converted into an art gallery in the early 20th century by Edward Raczyński (Count, politician, and later President of Poland in exile), who installed a collection of Polish and European painting; the oaks of Rogalin — including the three ancient named specimens Lech, Czech, and Rus — are the most famous living feature of the estate

opening_hours.seasonal_note: Open Tuesday–Sunday April through October; winter hours vary (November–March limited access, some areas closed). The art gallery in the coach house and the formal garden have their own access points. The English landscape park and oak grove are accessible year-round during daylight hours. Confirm current times at rogalin.muzeum.poznan.pl.

visit_duration: 1.5–2 hours (palace interior, art gallery, formal garden, and walk to the oak grove)
best_season: May to September — the English landscape park is at its best in spring and summer; the ancient oak grove is impressive in full leaf (May–October). Autumn gives the park good colour. The palace interior is worthwhile year-round in the open season.
accessibility: The palace interior involves stairs and period flooring. The art gallery in the coach house has level access. The formal garden is accessible on gravel paths; the English landscape park and oak grove require walking on uneven grass and natural ground. The GYG private tour from Poznań includes transport but the site's physical terrain cannot be altered.
tagline: The Raczyński family's Baroque palace in Greater Poland — and the home of three ancient named oaks (Lech, Czech, and Rus) that are among Europe's most celebrated living natural monuments
highlights: Three ancient named oaks: Lech, Czech, and Rus — the oak grove at Rogalin contains over 1,000 ancient trees, including three specimens named after the legendary brothers who founded the Polish, Czech, and Rus' nations according to medieval myth; these three trees, several centuries old with trunks several metres in circumference, became national symbols of Slavic cultural continuity during the Polish romantic period; they are living monuments in every sense — protected, individually identified, and visited by Poles who regard them as the arboreal equivalent of historical landmarks

The Raczyński art collection — Polish painting and European masters — the coach house of the Rogalin estate was converted in the early 20th century by Edward Raczyński into an art gallery housing the family's collection; the gallery includes significant works of Polish painting — Jan Matejko (the canonical painter of Polish historical subjects in the romantic era), Jacek Malczewski, Józef Brandt, and others — alongside European paintings of the 17th and 18th centuries; the collection, administered by the National Museum in Poznań, gives Rogalin an art gallery dimension unusual among estate museum visits

Baroque palace of a major Polish aristocratic family — the Raczyński family were one of the most prominent noble clans in Greater Poland across the 18th and 19th centuries; Kazimierz Raczyński, who built the palace in the 1770s–80s, was Voivode of Greater Poland; Edward Raczyński (1786–1845) was a collector, bibliophile, and supporter of Polish culture; Count Edward Raczyński (1891–1993), who donated the estate to Poland, was President of the Republic of Poland in exile from 1979 to 1986

English landscape park — the estate grounds include a formal French garden adjacent to the palace and an extensive English landscape park of several dozen hectares, with mature specimen trees, natural meadows, and the famous ancient oak grove; the park is accessible year-round and is one of the most pleasant walking landscapes of any Polish estate

Natural pairing with Kórnik Castle — Rogalin and Kórnik Castle are approximately 10km apart and routinely combined in a half-day excursion from Poznań; the GYG private tour (t26512) covers both with hotel pickup, transport, guide, and entrance tickets in a four-hour programme
description:
The three oaks named Lech, Czech, and Rus are the most immediately graspable thing about Rogalin for a visitor unfamiliar with the estate. They stand in the English landscape park that extends beyond the palace's formal French garden — three trees of several centuries' growth, their trunks several metres in circumference, their canopies occupying a substantial section of the park. The names were given during the Polish romantic period of the 19th century, when the triple brotherhood of the legendary Slavic founders (Lech, ancestor of the Poles; Czech, ancestor of the Czechs; Rus, ancestor of the Eastern Slavs) became a patriotic symbol for a culture under foreign administration. The oaks at Rogalin, already old by the 19th century, were given the names as a way of anchoring national myth to living, physical reality — a particularly Polish way of asserting continuity at a time when Poland's political existence was suspended.

The park that contains the three oaks holds over a thousand ancient trees in total, including many other oak specimens of significant age. The management of this grove — protecting trees that are simultaneously natural monuments and living organisms subject to disease and collapse — is a continuous conservation effort that has been ongoing since the Raczyński family donated the estate to the Polish state in the mid-20th century. Walking among the ancient oaks, which stand in an irregular formation across open parkland that allows their canopies full room to develop, gives a physical sense of the scale of time that no interior museum exhibit can replicate.

The palace itself was built in the 1770s and 1780s for Kazimierz Raczyński, Voivode of Greater Poland — one of the senior administrative positions in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth of the pre-partition era. The architecture is Baroque in the Central European aristocratic tradition, with flanking wings and service buildings added in the early 19th century that extended the estate composition without disturbing the coherence of the main building. The formal French garden adjacent to the palace provides the geometric counterpoint to the naturalistic English park beyond — the canonical dual composition of 18th-century aristocratic estate design in Central Europe.

The art collection installed in the former coach house of the estate is one of the most significant aspects of Rogalin that visitors routinely underestimate. Edward Raczyński (1886–1945), who converted the coach house into a gallery in the early 20th century, was building on a family tradition of collecting that went back several generations. The gallery includes works by the canonical painters of Polish romantic nationalism — Jan Matejko, whose large-format historical canvases defined how 19th-century Poles visualised their medieval past; Jacek Malczewski, the symbolist painter of Polish historical consciousness; Józef Brandt, the painter of Polish cavalry and steppe landscapes — alongside European paintings and decorative arts. The collection is administered by the National Museum in Poznań, which also manages the palace and grounds.

The Raczyński family's connection to Polish public life continued beyond the estate. Count Edward Raczyński (1891–1993) — the grandson of the gallery's founder — had a remarkable biographical trajectory: Polish ambassador to Britain in 1939, a figure of the Polish government in exile during the Second World War, and President of the Republic of Poland in exile from 1979 to 1986, at the age of 88. He died in London in 1993, two years after the Polish republic was restored. He had earlier donated the Rogalin estate, along with its collection and grounds, to the Polish state — a gesture that preserved what the private family could no longer maintain and ensured the estate's public accessibility.

Rogalin Palace and Kórnik Castle are approximately 10 kilometres apart and are covered together by the GYG half-day private tour from Poznań (t26512). The two sites present complementary aspects of Greater Poland's aristocratic heritage: Rogalin with its Baroque palace, art gallery, and ancient oak grove; Kórnik with its neo-Gothic transformation, Moorish Hall, and historic library.

[Kórnik Castle](/castles/poland/kornik-castle) — Karl Friedrich Schinkel's neo-Gothic masterpiece 10km east, the Działyński family's castle of Polish cultural resistance with an Alhambra-inspired Moorish Hall and Poland's oldest arboretum — is the natural companion visit. [Wilanów Palace](/castles/poland/wilanow-palace) — the Baroque royal residence near Warsaw built for King Jan III Sobieski, one of Poland's grandest palace-and-garden compositions — is the major reference point for readers exploring Poland's aristocratic palace circuit more broadly.
history: Late 18th century (c. 1770–90): Kazimierz Raczyński, Voivode of Greater Poland, builds the Baroque palace at Rogalin; formal French garden and initial park established. Early 19th century: flanking wings and service buildings added; English landscape park extended; ancient oak grove incorporated into the estate's designed landscape. 19th century: Raczyński family develops the estate and its collections across successive generations; the ancient oaks acquire their legendary names (Lech, Czech, Rus) as symbols of Slavic national identity. Early 20th century: Edward Raczyński converts the coach house into an art gallery; major Polish and European paintings installed. 1939–1945: Second World War; estate survives; some collections evacuated or at risk. Mid-20th century: Count Edward Raczyński (later President of Poland in exile) donates the estate to the Polish state; National Museum in Poznań established as administrator. Present day: palace, art gallery, and park open Tuesday–Sunday; oak grove accessible year-round.
how_to_visit:
**GYG half-day private tour (~$77/person, t26512, 4 hours):** Private tour from Poznań hotel pickup covering Rogalin Palace and gardens plus Kórnik Castle in the same half-day; transportation, guide, and entrance to both sites included. 5.0★ / 2 reviews. Best for visitors wanting guided context for both the palace history and the art collection.

**Independent visit:** Entry approximately 40–50 PLN (adults), open Tuesday–Sunday April–October (winter access limited). Rogalin is approximately 25km south of Poznań by road; easiest by car (approximately 35 minutes). Limited public transport from Poznań — bus or taxi from Mosina (approximately 5km) is the best option without a car. Allow 1.5–2 hours for palace, gallery, and oak grove.

**Visiting in context:** Combine with Kórnik Castle (10km east, approximately 10 minutes by car) for a Greater Poland aristocratic half-day from Poznań. The two sites together — Baroque palace plus neo-Gothic castle — give a complete picture of Greater Poland's 18th and 19th-century aristocratic culture.

faqs.question: Who are Lech, Czech, and Rus, and why are the oaks at Rogalin named after them?
faqs.answer: Lech, Czech, and Rus are the legendary brothers of medieval Slavic mythology — the eponymous founders of the Poles (Lech), Czechs (Czech), and East Slavs/Rus' (Rus). The myth of the three brothers appears in medieval chronicles and became a significant motif in 19th-century Polish romantic nationalism, when Polish intellectuals and artists were working to preserve a sense of national identity under Russian, Prussian, and Austrian partition. The three most impressive ancient oaks at Rogalin were given these names in the romantic period as a way of connecting living natural monuments to national mythological identity. The oaks are genuinely ancient — several centuries old — and their size and age made them natural candidates for this kind of symbolic naming. Today they are among the most famous trees in Poland.

faqs.question: What is in the Rogalin art gallery?
faqs.answer: The Rogalin art gallery, housed in the former coach house of the estate and administered by the National Museum in Poznań, contains Polish painting from the 19th and early 20th centuries alongside European decorative arts and paintings. The Polish collection includes works by Jan Matejko (historical paintings defining Polish romantic nationalist iconography), Jacek Malczewski (symbolist canvases drawing on Polish historical memory), Józef Brandt (cavalry and steppe subjects), and other figures of the Polish romantic and late-19th-century tradition. The gallery gives Rogalin a museum dimension that goes beyond a purely architectural or estate visit — it is a significant collection in its own right, accessible as part of the Rogalin estate ticket.

faqs.question: Can Rogalin and Kórnik Castle be visited in the same half-day from Poznań?
faqs.answer: Yes — Rogalin and Kórnik Castle are approximately 10km apart and are designed as a combined visit in the GYG private tour (t26512), which covers both in four hours from a Poznań hotel with guide, transport, and entrance tickets included. Independent visitors can drive between the two sites in approximately 10–15 minutes. The two sites complement each other well: Rogalin is a Baroque estate with an art gallery and ancient oak grove; Kórnik is a neo-Gothic castle with an Alhambra-inspired interior and historic library. Together they cover a wide range of Greater Poland's aristocratic heritage in a single morning or afternoon.
